newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan seeks apology from U.S. attorney.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan seeks apology from U.S. attorney.

text.p: Pakistan called in U.S. ambassador Thomas Simons on Monday and said it was still waiting for an apology from an American lawyer whose remarks about Pakistan have caused a national outcry.

The remarks were reportedly made by Virginia Commonwealth attorney Robert Horan after June's arrest of Pakistan's Mir Aimal Kansi for his alleged role in a 1993 shooting spree outside CIA headquarters in Langley, Virginia in which two men died.
Ambassador Simons was told by the Foreign Ministry that the apology was "still awaited," a ministry statement said. Pakistan has already lodged a formal protest to the U.S.

Pakistani newspapers have quoted Horan as saying in a June 23 television interview that people in the region where Kansi lived were backward and could sell their mothers for a far lesser amount than the $2 million award Washington had promised for his arrest.
On Sunday, Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif called the remarks "uncivilised, irrational, unwarranted and against decent norms and values of humanity".
On Monday, state radio quoted President Farooq Leghari as telling local reporters that the attorney's remarks "smelled of racism".
The Foreign Ministry said the U.S. State Department had expressed sincere regrets and informed Islamabad that it had advised Horan to retract and issue a public apology.

Kansi, a native of the mainly tribal southwestern province of Baluchistan bordering Afghanistan and Iran, was captured by agents of the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) with the help of Pakistani commandos in a mysterious operation that had itself sparked protests inside the country.
Some politicians accused Sharif's government of compromising national sovereignty by handing over a Pakistani to a foreign government without meeting legal formalities for extradition.
Islamabad has still not explained its role in the capture of Kansi, the prime suspect for the 1993 shooting.

The FBI said at the time Kansi had been delivered abroad by unidentified Afghan individuals to the custody of U.S. authorities, and that he had been brought to the Virginia suburb of Fairfax to face trial.
